topics.title: Puppy problem
topics.text:
Ian's Pomeranian had a litter of puppies. Ian, a building statistician decided to keep track of some data about the puppies. Here is some information Ian collected about his puppies.



There were 4 female and 3 male puppies in the litter.

The median birth weight of the puppies was 14 ounces.

The mean birth weight of puppies was 15 ounces.

The mode of the birth weight was 14 ounces.

The range of the birth weight was 8 ounces.



Show all work.

1. Determine the possible weights for Ian's puppies. Find another set of puppy weights that match the information given. Explain your strategy.



2. Ian weighed the puppies 1 week after they were born. He discovered that all puppies had gained exactly 8 ounces. How will the median, mean, mode, and rage of the puppies' weights compare to those of the puppies' weights at birth?



3. Ian weighed the puppies again after another week. He discovered that 3 of the puppies had each gained 10 ounces, 2 puppies had each gained 15 ounces, and 2 puppies that were sick each lost 3 ounces. What was the mean weight of the puppies after the weighing.

topics.title: k MATHCOUNTS For Summer
topics.text:
In MATHCOUNTS, practice is important. If you don't put effort into solving problems as prep work, you will never go far. But I think all of you know this already. The thing is, sometimes, getting the practice problems is hard. They can cost a lot of money. I am offering this   for free  because I think it is important for MATHCOUNTS to be a competition that doesn't have a clear favorite. At this past year's Nats, Luke's written score of 44 was 4 points better than Andrew's second place score of 40. Just like sports, wouldn't it be more exciting if it was a tie; if you didn't actually have a good prediction of who was going to win? This is why, as a quarterfinalist from the 2017-2018 National Competition, I would like to help teach the next generation of MATHCOUNTS participants.



This summer, I am giving the first **16 Signups** a chance to practice by solving national-level MATHCOUNTS problems 5 days a week, and learn important tricks and shortcuts to the competition in general. A private forum will be made for these 16 people, and if you just can't solve a problem, I will work through it with you 1 on 1. But, if I find someone is trolling, there will be no second chances, and that person will be immediately kicked out and replaced by the next in line. If there are already 16 signups, but you wanted to participate,  sign up anyways  and you could take the place of a troll. Depending on popularity, I might even allow more people, who knows?



Please signup in the normal format: Signups(0)




** This is now changed!! Signups do not have a numerical limit, instead signups simply end Monday morning 10:00 AM EST



Private forum can be found here:

https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c663718_mathcounts_summer_practice



EDIT: Signups are now closed!!

topics.title: Can someone check my proofs for these theorems??
topics.text:
Ptomely's Theorem: (Assume that we have a cyclic quadrilateral $ABCD$ inscribed in a circle already drawn) To start



our proof let us locate a point P such that $\angle ACB = \angle PCD$  Because angles $BAC$ and $BDC$ are part of



a cyclic quadrilateral they must subtend the same arc. This means we have $\angle BAC = \angle BDC$. Because



$\angle BAC = \angle BDC$ and $\angle ACB = \angle PCD$ we have $\triangle ABC \sim \triangle DPC$. Therefore



we have. $\frac{CD}{PD}=\frac{AC}{AB}$. Cross multiplying we have $CD*AB = PD*AC$.



Using a similar method we have $\triangle BCP \sim \triangle ACD$ using $\angle BCP = \angle ACD$. This gives us



$BC*AD=AC*BM$. Now we can add our final equations to have $CD*AB+BC*AD = AC*BP+PD*AC = AC*BD$.

topics.text:
You are on a gameshow, with three doors. Behind one is a goat, behind another is a car, and behind the last is a goat with a radioactive element in a container and a Geiger counter. If any atom of the radioactive isotope has decayed (with 50% probability), then the goat will mutate into a car. To play, you have to choose a door, and then the announcer will open the door most likely to have a goat, which is not the one you chose. Then, he will give you the option of switching or staying with your choice. (If he opens the door and it is a car, you win.)

Unfortunately, he opens the door and it is a goat. Should you switch or stay to maximize your chance at getting a car?

topics.title: Water Bottle Problem
topics.text:
ProblemThere is a cylinder filled halfway with water. The cylinder has radius $A$ centimeters and height $B$ centimeters. The cylinder is placed into a holder, that snugly contains the cylinder. A point on the center of the water bottle is attached to a lever. The lever, cylinder, and water within the cylinder is currently in a perfectly upright position. When the lever is rotated $C$ radians, what is the surface area of the water's surface? Express your answer in terms of $A$, $B$, and $C$. (Try experimenting with a water bottle and see what will happen)

Challenge: Find the average surface area of the water, as C varies through all real numbers, in terms of A and B.


Strategies for Solving Problem - Don't open unless you are stuck.Trig and Pythagorean Theorem


SolutionThe water's surface has 2 different shapes, based on $C$. It could be either an ellipse or a rectangle. But when does the shape of the water surface changed? Well, try rotating a water bottle. The shape of the water's surface is a rectangle when the top and bottom bases of the cylinder touches the water's surface. If the water's surface doesn't come in contact with the bases, then the water's surface will be an ellipse. The area of an ellipse is equal to $\pi*r_1*r_2$, where $r_1$ and $r_2$ are the two different semi-axes of the ellipse. (The two different "radii") Observe that the length of one of the axes always stays the same: it remains at 2A, so its semi-axis is A. The other radius can be found using trigonometry and the Pythagorean Theorem. Draw in the two surfaces of water: one rotated, and one in the stationary position. Then, take the cross-section of the cylinder, then drop an altitude from the tip of the rotated surface and place the foot of the altitude on the edge of the stationary surface. The side opposite of the angle formed by the intersecting surfaces is $\tan(C)*A$ Thus, the radius's length is equal to $\sqrt{\tan^2(C)+1}*A$, by the Pythagorean Theorem. Therefore, the formula for the area of the water's surface when its shape is an ellipse is $\sqrt{\tan^2(C)+1}*A^2*\pi$cm$^2$ = $\frac{A^2\pi}{\cos(C)}$

The surface area when it's an rectangle is way simpler. Draw the two right triangles (same as before), and we find the length of the right triangle is equal to $2*\sqrt{\frac{B^2}{4}+\frac{B^2}{4\tan^2(C)}} = \frac{B*\sqrt{\tan^2(C)+1}}{tan(C)}=\frac{B}{sin(C)}$. The width is simply $2A$. Hence, the area is $\frac{2AB}{\sin(C)}$.

Hence, the answer is:

For $C$ $\le$ $\arctan{\frac{A}{2B}}$:

$\frac{A^2*\pi}{\cos(C)}$cm$^2$

For $C$ $>$ $\arctan{\frac{A}{2B}}$:

$\frac{2AB}{\sin(C)}$
